title: The allow rule is right there, so why is HTTPS blocked? (NSG priority)
intro: At 09:41 the web tier stopped receiving traffic. The rule 'Allow-HTTPS' (443 from Internet) is still in nsg-web, unchanged. bob says his change 'only added a rule to block a scanner'.

steps.prompt: Ask Network Watcher whether inbound TCP from 203.0.113.9:50000 to vm-web-01 (10.20.1.4:443) in rg-web-prod is allowed.
expected_commands: az network watcher test-ip-flow --resource-group rg-web-prod --vm vm-web-01 --direction Inbound --protocol TCP --local 10.20.1.4:443 --remote 203.0.113.9:50000
az network watcher test-ip-flow -g rg-web-prod --vm vm-web-01 --direction Inbound --protocol TCP --local 10.20.1.4:443 --remote 203.0.113.9:50000
steps.hint: IP flow verify names the rule that decided.

steps.prompt: Denied by Block-Scanner, bob's new rule. List the rules of nsg-web (rg-web-prod) to see it next to Allow-HTTPS.
expected_commands: az network nsg rule list --resource-group rg-web-prod --nsg-name nsg-web --output table
az network nsg rule list -g rg-web-prod --nsg-name nsg-web -o table
steps.fake_output:
Name          Priority  Direction  Access  Protocol  SourceAddressPrefix  DestinationPortRange
------------  --------  ---------  ------  --------  -------------------  --------------------
Block-Scanner 90        Inbound    Deny    *         *                    *
Allow-HTTPS   100       Inbound    Allow   Tcp       Internet             443
steps.hint: Compare the priorities, and look at the source of the Deny rule.

steps.prompt: Block-Scanner (priority 90, evaluated first) denies source '*', which is everyone, instead of the scanner's IP. Fix it so it only blocks 192.0.2.66: update Block-Scanner's source prefix in nsg-web.
expected_commands: az network nsg rule update --resource-group rg-web-prod --nsg-name nsg-web --name Block-Scanner --source-address-prefixes 192.0.2.66
az network nsg rule update -g rg-web-prod --nsg-name nsg-web -n Block-Scanner --source-address-prefixes 192.0.2.66

steps.prompt: Re-run the same IP flow verify from 203.0.113.9:50000 to 10.20.1.4:443 on vm-web-01.
expected_commands: az network watcher test-ip-flow --resource-group rg-web-prod --vm vm-web-01 --direction Inbound --protocol TCP --local 10.20.1.4:443 --remote 203.0.113.9:50000
az network watcher test-ip-flow -g rg-web-prod --vm vm-web-01 --direction Inbound --protocol TCP --local 10.20.1.4:443 --remote 203.0.113.9:50000
steps.hint: Same command as the first step.

steps.prompt: Check the scanner itself is still blocked: test from 192.0.2.66:50000 to 10.20.1.4:443.
expected_commands: az network watcher test-ip-flow --resource-group rg-web-prod --vm vm-web-01 --direction Inbound --protocol TCP --local 10.20.1.4:443 --remote 192.0.2.66:50000
az network watcher test-ip-flow -g rg-web-prod --vm vm-web-01 --direction Inbound --protocol TCP --local 10.20.1.4:443 --remote 192.0.2.66:50000
steps.hint: Test both what should be allowed and what should be blocked.

resolution: NSG rules are evaluated by priority, lowest first, and the first match wins. Allow-HTTPS was 'right there' but never reached, because Block-Scanner at priority 90 matched first. That was fine in principle (deny rules for specific bad actors belong above allow rules), but its source was left as '*' (probably the portal's default), so it denied the entire internet. IP flow verify found the exact rule in one command. Verify firewall changes both ways: that legitimate traffic still passes and that the blocked traffic is really blocked. Better still, manage NSGs in Terraform or Bicep so a change like this shows a readable diff ('source: 192.0.2.66' vs '*') in code review before it's applied.
